newsitem.title: GABON: Mobutu will return to Kinshasa Saturday, son says.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu will return to Kinshasa Saturday, son says.

text.p: Zaire's embattled president, Mobutu Sese Seko, will fly home to his capital Kinshasa on Saturday and suggestions to the contrary are intended to sow panic, his son and spokesman Nzanga Mobutu said.
"People outside (Zaire) are saying that President Mobutu will go into exile. This is to bring panic. They do not know the president," Nzanga told Reuters in Gabon's capital Libreville late on Friday.

"He is still convalescing. All his life he has fought for the territorial integrity of his country," he said in the interview at the small but plush hotel Le Maicha belonging to Mobutu's daughter Chantalle on the edge of Libreville airfield.
Mobutu, 66, who is battling cancer and Laurent Kabila's rebels, has dominated Zaire for over three decades.
But the rebels have won control of three-quarters of the huge and potentially rich nation since October and have threatened to chase him from Kinshasa unless he resigns.
Asked where the veteran leader would travel on Saturday, Nzanga replied: "To Kinshasa."
Mobutu met fellow French-speaking Central African leaders in Libreville on Thursday and they called for Zaire's transitional parliament to have a role in a peaceful settlement of the civil war.

He had been due to return to Kinshasa on Friday but Nzanga said he stayed in Gabon for talks with South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who met Kabila on Friday at rebel headquarters in Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi.

"The president postponed his departure from today because we were supposed to meet Deputy President Mbeki," Nzanga said. "Mr Mbeki was supposed to come earlier but the meeting was postponed until tomorrow."
Nzanga denied reports that rebels had captured and ransacked Mobutu's jungle palace at Gbadolite. "Gbadolite has not fallen. I spoke to people there today," he said.
Independent witnesses, in the form of foreign journalists, found it peaceful and under government control on Friday.
Kabila and his rebels, who took up arms in a dispute over nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority, say they will take Kinshasa but little has been heard from the battle front in recent days.
Nzanga said his father would not accept bloodshed and, throwing his weight behind a democratic settlement to the war, he said: "Zairean people have the right to choose their leader."

He said he believed the Kinshasa authorities had had a bad deal from the international press. "The general feeling in Kinshasa is that the international media report anything that the rebellion is saying," he said.
Mobutu and Kabila met last Sunday at talks hosted by South African President Nelson Mandela on a South African ship and Mbeki is trying to arrange follow-up negotiations.

"I suppose he met Kabila back there (in Lubumbashi) and he will probably make a proposal for a timeframe for the next meeting," Nzanga said. Kabila has already agreed to meet Mobutu again next Wednesday under South African mediation.
